messages.subject: Is this package appropriate for my dataset?
parts:
Hello,
A reviewer recommended this package to expand the analysis in my manuscript beyond Minimum Convex Polygon. After playing around with the package and reading the various supporting material, now I'm not so sure that my dataset lends itself to this analysis. I manually radio-tracked tortoises and recorded observations via GPS. Tracking duration ranged from 4-6 months, in which time I obtained 29-50 fixes on each individual. Intervals between fixes ranged between 2~6 days. Individuals did exhibit fidelity to certain areas, although repeat observations in the same location may not represent 'autocorrelation' in the same sense that two fixes one hour apart do.

I see that the timestamp is a necessary datum for each fix, and upon examining the 'Buffalo' dataset, I noticed the timestamp values range between 5:00~59:00. Being unfamiliar with this type of tracking and MoveBank, it doesn't seem like the date is associated with each fix, is that correct? Does the package take into account the date and time of the fix, or just the time (i.e., is the autocorrelation that is being addressed only across the span of a couple of hours within the same day)?

Thank you for any comments directed toward my specific situation and in satisfying my general curiosity in the package.

Ross Couvillon

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Is this package appropriate for my dataset?
parts:
Hi Ross,

I don't know what species you are working with, but I know from experience that both Sonoran and Galapogos tortoises take a couple of weeks to cross their range, and so for them a 2-6 day sampling interval would give rise to some autocorrelation.

When autocorrelation is not present in the data, home-range analysis in ctmm automatically reduces to an IID KDE, but with a couple of bias corrections that will help with smaller sample sizes (29-50 fixes is small for nonparametric methods like KDE and MCP). Even with IID data, the default method in ctmm is more statistically efficient than conventional KDE methods used in ecology, so there's still a benefit to using it. You can also account for telemetry error in ctmm, which can be important in some datasets regardless of autocorrelation.

The full date-time is used in ctmm. You might be looking at a dataset from another R package. Try data('buffalo',package='ctmm') or without capitalizing 'buffalo'. Autocorrelation timescales can be of any duration. The package has been tested on species from bacterium to whales. Everything is rescaled internally for numerical stability and output units can range from microns to kilometers.

Best,
Chris

parts:
Hi Dr. Fleming,
I appreciate the insights. I've explored the package on and off and have attempted to find the home range for two Texas Tortoises I've monitored. This species has been described as “primarily nomadic, and maintain restricted activity ranges for only a few days between successive greater or lesser secondary movements.” In my experience they maintain more fidelity than that characterization, but it's still apt and perhaps is the reason why calculating the home range for these individuals has not been been cut and dry.

For tortoise #2, the variogram (image 1) levels off (mostly) but then plummets near the very end of sampling. The OU anisotropic model had the lowest AICc score, but as you can see from the second and third images (long and short duration variograms, respectively) the model fit is a little sloppy. The close match between the fitted model and empirical variogram in the Calabrese et al. 2016 Cilla example has me wondering if this is somehow off (although this is a better fit than the next models with the closest AICc score).

 

For tortoise #10, I see the opposite and the leveled off variogram spikes towards the end of sampling. I get "Warning message: In cov.loglike(hess, grad) : MLE is near a boundary or optim() failed." because the maximum likelihood for T(velocity) is 0.  I've tried to obtain GUESS by 
1) variogram.fit(vg.tortoise10) by itself and followed by variogram.fit(vg.tortoise10,CTMM=GUESS) 
2) ctmm.guess(tortoise10) by itself and followed by ctmm.guess(tortoise10,CTMM=GUESS)

but the call fitted.mods<-ctmm.select(tortoise10,CTMM=GUESS,verbose=TRUE) returns the warning message. For what it's worth, the top fitted model WITH the warning is OUf isotropic. Not sure what I should try next. 


I appreciate any help you can offer. 

Regards,
Ross

parts:
Hi Ross,

Tortoise #2 looks good. The tail end of the variogram has very little data and very wide confidence intervals. Don't worry too much about it.
Tortoise #10 looks okay. There appears to be a little bit of range shifting or other non-stationarity in the data that causes the variogram to slowly creep upwards just after 2 months of lag, but its not a terrible fit for the stationary model. You might want to look further and see what was going on there.

The warning you got is not important if you are using ctmm.select (and not ctmm.fit directly) and I am right now putting in code to detect that and not issue the warning if ctmm.select is being used. Don't expect to be able to support any model feature in any dataset. However, for this data you might benefit from an error model, because the scale of movement is so small. See vignette('error').

Best,
Chris

The current movement models in ctmm are stationary, so in situations like that you do need to segment the data.

Best,
Chris

On Tuesday, September 3, 2019 at 8:39:27 AM UTC-5, Christen Fleming wrote:
Hi Ross,

I don't know what species you are working with, but I know from experience that both Sonoran and Galapogos tortoises take a couple of weeks to cross their range, and so for them a 2-6 day sampling interval would give rise to some autocorrelation.

When autocorrelation is not present in the data, home-range analysis in ctmm automatically reduces to an IID KDE, but with a couple of bias corrections that will help with smaller sample sizes (29-50 fixes is small for nonparametric methods like KDE and MCP). Even with IID data, the default method in ctmm is more statistically efficient than conventional KDE methods used in ecology, so there's still a benefit to using it. You can also account for telemetry error in ctmm, which can be important in some datasets regardless of autocorrelation.

The full date-time is used in ctmm. You might be looking at a dataset from another R package. Try data('buffalo',package='ctmm') or without capitalizing 'buffalo'. Autocorrelation timescales can be of any duration. The package has been tested on species from bacterium to whales. Everything is rescaled internally for numerical stability and output units can range from microns to kilometers.

Best,
Chris

On Friday, January 17, 2020 at 5:05:04 PM UTC-6, Christen Fleming wrote:
Hi Ross,

If you take 2 segments from one movement process, estimate them separately under the assumption of two movement processes and re-combine them afterwards, then you give up statistical efficiency, but there should be a lot of overlap.

If you take 2 movement processes, like summer range and winter range behavior, and estimate them under the assumption of a single stationary process, then the result will be biased too big. The current movement models in ctmm are stationary, so in situations like that you do need to segment the data.
